questions.q: In the case study's workflow, why does the checkout step use fetch-depth: 0?
options: To speed up the checkout with no other purpose
Because GitHub requires it on every workflow
Because the delta-deployment step (sf sgd source delta) needs full Git history to compute a diff between commits
It has no connection to any other step in the pipeline
questions.explain: fetch-depth: 0 pulls full history, which the sgd source delta step depends on to diff HEAD against HEAD~1 -- the same reason given in Lesson 10.

questions.q: In the walked-through incident (a trigger referencing a field missing from the same PR), where does this lesson say the problem is actually most likely to surface?
options: The static analysis (PMD) step, since missing dependencies are a code-quality pattern PMD checks for
Nowhere -- this pipeline as designed cannot catch this kind of error at all
Only during the production quick-deploy step, never earlier
The delta-deploy step, which fails with a component-level error naming the missing field reference, blocking the pull request's required check
questions.explain: A missing-dependency error is a deploy-time failure, not a static-analysis pattern -- the delta deploy step is where this specific scenario surfaces and fails the required check.

questions.q: What does the environment: production setting on the release-to-production job enforce, per Lesson 5's pattern reused here?
options: It automatically disables all Apex tests for speed
It deletes the production org's existing metadata first
It requires a named reviewer's approval before the job is allowed to run, serving as a deliberate human gate on the actual release
It has no real effect; it's purely cosmetic labeling
questions.explain: A GitHub Actions environment with required reviewers pauses the job until a named person approves it -- the Continuous Delivery pattern of automating everything up to a deliberate, human-approved release.

questions.q: What does this lesson say the pipeline would NOT catch on its own, even with every gate passing?
options: Apex test coverage below 75%
A missing dependency in the delta manifest
A failed JWT authentication step
Whether the trigger's business logic is actually correct -- passing tests only prove the code does what its own tests say it should, not that those tests encode the right requirement
questions.explain: Automated gates verify that code satisfies its own tests and checks -- they can't verify the tests themselves encode the correct business requirement, which is why code review still matters alongside automation.

questions.q: What does the needs: validate setting on the release-to-production job do?
options: It makes release-to-production run before validate, regardless of order
It duplicates the validate job's steps automatically
It creates a job-level dependency ensuring release-to-production only runs after the validate job has succeeded
It has no effect on execution order
questions.explain: needs: establishes a dependency between jobs -- release-to-production waits for validate to succeed before it's allowed to start.
